title: The due of the dead (geras thanontōn)
greek: ὃ γὰρ γέρας ἐστὶ θανόντων (ho gar geras esti thanontōn)
short: Mourning is a 'privilege' (geras) owed to the dead, the same word used of a warrior's prize of honour; Akhilleus leads the Myrmidons three times round the corpse.
body: Geras is the word for the special share of honour a chief receives from the spoils, the very thing whose loss (Briseis) started Akhilleus' wrath in Book I. Here it is transferred to the dead: lament, the funeral and a tomb are what the community owes them, and the formula recurs elsewhere for the barrow and the tombstone (16.457, 16.675) and the cut hair and tears of mourners (Od. 4.197-8). Akhilleus at once performs the first of these rites: the Myrmidons drive their chariots three times round the body (23.13), a ritual circling that Leaf compares with the later dragging of Hector round the barrow (24.16) and that is repeated, by armed men, at Akhilleus' own funeral (Od. 24.68-70). Book XXIII is in this sense a sequence of gerea: lament, feast, pyre, barrow and games, each paid in turn. The irony, sharpened in Book XXIV, is that Akhilleus pays the dead their due while denying it to Hector.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 23.9 and 23.13
LSJ s.v. γέρας

anchor: Hail, I bid thee, O Patroclus
title: Akhilleus' farewell to Patroclus: 'Hail, even in the house of Hades'
greek: χαῖρέ μοι ὦ Πάτροκλε καὶ εἰν Ἀΐδαο δόμοισι (chaire moi, ō Patrokle, kai ein Aïdao domoisi)
short: Akhilleus greets the dead man as if he could hear, and promises the two terrible offerings of the book: Hector to the dogs and twelve Trojan youths at the pyre.
body: Chaire is the everyday Greek greeting ('rejoice', 'hail'), later the standard word on gravestones; Leaf notes the force of 'even in Hades', where there is little to rejoice in. The address treats Patroclus as still present and able to receive gifts. Akhilleus says he is now 'fulfilling' what he promised (the vow of 18.333-7), and the promise has two parts: Hector's body thrown raw to dogs, and twelve noble Trojan youths beheaded before the pyre (taken alive for this purpose at 21.26-32). The same two lines return word for word when the pyre is lit (23.179-83), where the human sacrifice is carried out and the threat to Hector's body is answered at once by the gods' protection of it. The speech frames the whole funeral as revenge as much as mourning; Book XXIV will close the frame when Akhilleus again addresses Patroclus 'in the house of Hades', this time to excuse the return of Hector's body (24.592-5).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 23.19-21 and 23.179-80

title: The ghost of Patroclus
greek: ψυχὴ Πατροκλῆος δειλοῖο (psychē Patroklēos deiloio)
short: Patroclus' psychē appears in a dream, asks for quick burial so he can cross into Hades, and asks that their bones share one urn.
body: This is the Iliad's only full ghost scene. The psychē ('breath-soul', the thing that leaves a man at death) looks exactly like the living man, but it is stuck: the other souls, the 'phantoms (eidōla) of men worn out', keep it from crossing 'the River' until the body has had its 'due of fire'. Leaf takes the river to be the Styx, perhaps Oceanus, and notes the odd idea of wandering in Hades before passing its gates. The belief that the unburied dead cannot rest is the principle on which the whole last movement of the poem turns: it is why Patroclus must be burned and why Hector's family need his body. Patroclus also foretells Akhilleus' death under the walls of Troy, recalls their shared upbringing in Peleus' house, and asks for a common urn. Erwin Rohde and later Jan Bremmer used this scene as central evidence for early Greek ideas of the soul; compare Elpenor's ghost, who asks for burial in almost the same terms (Od. 11.51-78).

title: Opoeis (Opous) and Patroclus' exile
greek: ἐξ Ὀπόεντος (ex Opoentos); ἀνδροκτασίη (androktasiē, man-slaying)
short: Patroclus came to Peleus' house as a boy exile from Opoeis in Locris, after killing a playmate in a quarrel over knucklebones.
body: Opoeis, later Opus, was the chief town of the eastern (Opuntian) Locrians in central Greece; Akhilleus had promised Menoetius to bring his son home there (18.324-7). Here the ghost tells how he came to Phthia instead: as a child he killed 'the son of Amphidamas' in anger over a game of astragaloi (knucklebones, Murray's 'dice'), 'not meaning to'. Apollodorus later names the victim Clitonymus. The story shows the normal Homeric response to homicide: the killer goes into exile and is taken in by a powerful man, here Peleus, who made him Akhilleus' therapōn ('squire'; some scholars detect in the word an older sense of 'ritual substitute'). It also prepares one of the great similes of Book XXIV, where Priam entering Akhilleus' hut is compared to a man who has killed someone at home and arrives as a suppliant at a rich man's house (24.480-4). Akhilleus' closest friend was himself once such an exile, received with kindness.

sources.cite: Apollodorus, Library 3.13.8

title: Psychē and eidōlon: 'but no mind in it at all'
greek: ψυχὴ καὶ εἴδωλον, ἀτὰρ φρένες οὐκ ἔνι πάμπαν (psychē kai eidōlon, atar phrenes ouk eni pampan)
short: When Akhilleus tries to embrace the ghost, it slips away 'like smoke', squeaking; he concludes that something survives in Hades, a shade and image, but without wits.
body: Three words carry the scene. The psychē goes under the earth 'like smoke' (kapnos), and it goes tetriguia, 'squeaking' or 'gibbering', the sound of bats in the parallel passage on the suitors' souls (Od. 24.5-9); Leaf compares Hamlet's 'the sheeted dead / Did squeak and gibber'. Akhilleus' conclusion, that there is 'a psychē and an eidōlon (image), but phrenes (the seat of thought and feeling) are not in it at all', is the clearest Homeric statement of what survives death. Leaf points out that such vivid dream-appearances were central to anthropological theories of the origin of belief in the soul. The failed embrace is the model for Odysseus' three attempts to clasp his mother's shade (Od. 11.204-8) and, through that, for Aeneas and Creusa and Anchises in Virgil (Aen. 2.792-4, 6.700-2).

title: Akhilleus' hair offering and the river Spercheus
greek: ξανθὴν ἀπεκείρατο χαίτην (xanthēn apekeirato chaitēn); Σπερχειός (Sperkheios)
short: Akhilleus cuts the lock he had grown for his home river Spercheus and gives it to the dead Patroclus instead: an open admission that he will never return home.
body: Spercheus is the river of Phthia, Akhilleus' homeland in southern Thessaly. Peleus had vowed that when his son came home Akhilleus would cut his hair for the river and sacrifice a hecatomb and fifty rams at its sanctuary. Greek boys commonly grew a lock to be dedicated to a river god on coming of age; Leaf cites Aeschylus' Choephori 6-7, where Orestes offers one lock to the river Inachus 'for nurture' and another to his dead father in mourning, and Pausanias, who saw a statue of a boy cutting his hair for the Cephisus and remarked that Homer's lines show the custom was ancient (1.37.3). Akhilleus merges the two rites. Because 'I go not home' (ou neomai, the language of nostos), the lock meant for the river of his homeland goes into the pyre: the gift itself acknowledges his chosen fate, the short life with glory instead of the homecoming (9.410-16).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 23.141 and 23.148

anchor: a pyre of an hundred feet
title: The pyre of Patroclus and its offerings
greek: πυρὴν ἑκατόμπεδον (pyrēn hekatompedon)
short: A pyre a hundred feet each way, with fat-wrapped body, jars of honey and oil, four horses, two dogs and twelve captives: the most lavish funeral in Homer.
body: The pyre is 'a hundred feet this way and that', a number that marks grandeur rather than measurement. The offerings follow in order: sheep and cattle flayed, their fat wrapped round the corpse so it will burn well; two-handled jars (amphiphoreis) of honey and oil leaned against the bier, which Leaf connects with the pointed amphoras and the lekythoi later set round the dead in Attic funerals; four horses; two of Patroclus' nine 'table-dogs'; and twelve Trojan youths. Archaeologists have compared the scene with rich burials of the Early Iron Age, above all the building at Toumba, Lefkandi, in Euboea (tenth century BC), where horses were buried beside a cremated warrior. The poem presents all of this as extraordinary, matched only by Akhilleus' own funeral in Odyssey XXIV. Hector's funeral in Book XXIV will be told in a few lines with none of these excesses.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 23.171
Homer, Iliad 23.163-77; Odyssey 24.43-84

anchor: grim was the work he purposed
title: The killing of twelve Trojans at the pyre
greek: κακὰ δὲ φρεσὶ μήδετο ἔργα (kaka de phresi mēdeto erga)
short: Homer's only human sacrifice: Akhilleus cuts the throats of twelve captured Trojan youths, and the narrator calls the deeds kaka, 'evil' or 'grim'.
body: The twelve were taken alive at the river for this purpose (21.26-32). Readers have argued about the narrator's comment 'he devised kaka erga in his heart'. Leaf held that epic narration does not pass moral judgement and that kaka means only 'bad for the victims', comparing the same phrase used of Zeus (7.478); many recent critics read it as a rare authorial note of disapproval, matching Apollo's verdict on Akhilleus in 24.39-54. Plato in the Republic (3.391b) refused to believe Akhilleus capable of 'the slaughter of captives at the pyre' and of dragging Hector round the tomb, and wanted such stories banned. Whether the scene preserves a memory of real practice is also debated; Dennis Hughes' survey of human sacrifice in Greece discusses the Homeric passage among his evidence. The act shows Akhilleus' grief still turned outward into killing; only in Book XXIV does it turn into shared mourning.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 23.176
Plato, Republic 3.391b
Dennis D. Hughes, Human Sacrifice in Ancient Greece (London: Routledge, 1991)

title: The gods protect Hector's body
greek: ῥοδόεντι δὲ χρῖεν ἐλαίῳ ἀμβροσίῳ (rhodoenti de chrien elaiōi ambrosiōi)
short: Aphrodite keeps the dogs off and anoints Hector with rose-scented immortal oil; Apollo covers him with a cloud so the sun cannot wither the flesh.
body: Akhilleus' threat (23.182-3) is answered at once by the narrator: no dog will touch Hector. Aphrodite, the Trojans' protector, anoints the body with 'rosy, ambrosial' oil; Leaf notes the ancient belief that oil of roses preserved even wooden statues (Pausanias 9.41.7). Apollo spreads a dark cloud over it. Leaf records that some critics rejected these lines because they anticipate the dragging and ransom of Book XXIV, but they establish the theme that runs through the last book: the gods keep the corpse whole, as Thetis did for Patroclus (19.29-39) and Apollo for Sarpedon (16.667-83). Apollo shields it with the aegis (24.18-21), and Hermes later tells Priam that after twelve days it lies 'dewy-fresh', its wounds closed (24.411-23). Charles Segal traced this motif of the threatened and protected corpse through the whole poem.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 23.184-91 and 23.186
Charles Segal, The Theme of the Mutilation of the Corpse in the Iliad (Leiden: Brill, 1971)
Pausanias 9.41.7 (oil of roses as preservative)

anchor: North Wind and the West Wind
title: Boreas and Zephyrus at the pyre
greek: Βορέῃ καὶ Ζεφύρῳ (Boreēi kai Zephyrōi)
short: The pyre will not catch, so Akhilleus prays to the North and West Winds; Iris fetches them from a feast, and they blow all night.
body: Boreas, the north wind from Thrace, and Zephyrus, the west wind, are treated as persons who can be bribed with 'fair offerings' and libations. Iris, who usually carries Zeus' messages, here acts on her own, and finds the winds banqueting in Zephyrus' house; they all jump up and invite her to sit beside them. Leaf found an 'unmistakable touch of humour' in the scene and noted that her excuse, a feast among the Ethiopians at the stream of Oceanus, echoes Book I (1.423-4), where it explains the gods' absence. The winds 'come to the sea', raise the waves, and fan the pyre through the night, returning home over the Thracian sea at dawn (23.229-30). The episode lets the poem stretch the burning over a whole night, the time of Akhilleus' ceaseless libation and lament.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), Introduction to Book XXIII, p. 468, and notes on 23.200 and 23.206
Hesiod, Theogony 378-80 (the winds as children of Eos and Astraeus)

title: Simile: a father burning his son's bones
greek: ὡς δὲ πατὴρ οὗ παιδὸς ὀδύρεται ὀστέα καίων (hōs de patēr hou paidos odyretai ostea kaiōn)
short: Akhilleus mourning Patroclus is like a father burning the bones of a newly married son: the simile looks ahead to Priam, and to Peleus.
body: The comparison inverts the natural order: a father burning a son is the grief Greek thought treated as the worst of all. The son is a nymphios, newly wed; Leaf suggests the word was used of a husband until he had a son, so the dead man leaves no heir. Akhilleus 'creeps' (herpyzōn) round the pyre, a verb Leaf notes is used elsewhere only of the grieving Odysseus and the old Laertes. The simile has two forward echoes. Priam, a father who has lost Hector and must ransom his bones, will kneel to Akhilleus in Book XXIV; and Peleus, Akhilleus' own father, will lose his only son, as Akhilleus tells Priam (24.538-42). The image is one of several in which Homer joins Akhilleus and Priam through the figure of the bereaved father.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 23.223 and 23.225
C. W. Macleod, Homer: Iliad Book XXIV (Cambridge, 1982), Introduction

title: The golden urn and the barrow of Patroclus
greek: ἐν χρυσέῃ φιάλῃ καὶ δίπλακι δημῷ (en chryseēi phialēi kai diplaki dēmōi)
short: Patroclus' bones go into a golden vessel, wrapped in fat, to wait for Akhilleus' own; the barrow is to be built large later, for both men.
body: Akhilleus orders the bones gathered into a golden phialē, wrapped in a double layer of fat, until he himself 'is hidden in Hades'. Leaf observes that this cannot be the shallow phialē of classical art and must be a covered, two-handled vessel. Only a modest mound is to be raised now; the Achaeans who survive him are to build it 'broad and high'. The Odyssey completes the story: Agamemnon's shade tells Akhilleus that his bones were mixed with Patroclus' in a golden amphora given by Thetis, the work of Hephaestus, and laid under a great tomb on a headland of the Hellespont, visible from the sea (Od. 24.73-84). Line 23.92, in which the ghost asks for this very amphora, was rejected by Aristarchus as borrowed from that passage. Strabo (13.1.32) records the tombs of Akhilleus and Patroclus shown near Sigeum. Gregory Nagy argues that the poem keeps this future shared tomb (sēma) in view.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 23.92 and 23.243
Homer, Odyssey 24.71-84
Strabo, Geography 13.1.32
Gregory Nagy, The Ancient Greek Hero in 24 Hours (Harvard, 2013), Hour 7

anchor: from his ships brought forth prizes
title: The funeral games (athla) for Patroclus
greek: νηῶν δ' ἔκφερ' ἄεθλα (nēōn d' ekpher' aethla)
short: Akhilleus holds eight contests for Patroclus, offering prizes from his own ships: the model for every later epic games.
body: Funeral games were a real Greek custom: Nestor recalls competing at the games for Amarynceus (23.629-42), and Hesiod says he won a tripod at the games for Amphidamas of Chalcis (Works and Days 654-7). The prizes (aethla) are the goods of heroic society: tripods, cauldrons, horses, mules, oxen, skilled women and 'grey iron'. Leaf notes that the Homeric talent was of small value, which is why two talents of gold come only fourth. The eight events are the chariot race, boxing, wrestling, foot race, armed duel, weight-throw, archery and javelin. The games are also a social drama. Akhilleus, so long withdrawn, now presides as a generous arbiter who settles quarrels, gives extra prizes and finally honours Agamemnon himself; the warriors who fought for status in Book I now compete under rules. Virgil's games for Anchises (Aeneid V) and Statius' in Thebaid VI are modelled on this book.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), Introduction to Book XXIII, pp. 467-8, and note on 23.269 (value of the talent)

Hesiod, Works and Days 654-7

anchor: For him they stand and mourn
title: Akhilleus' immortal horses mourn their charioteer
greek: τὸν τώ γ' ἑσταότες πενθείετον (ton tō g' hestaotes pentheieton)
short: Akhilleus will not race: his immortal horses, a gift of Poseidon to Peleus, stand grieving for Patroclus with their manes trailing on the ground.
body: The horses are Xanthus and Balius, immortal offspring of the West Wind and the Harpy Podarge (16.148-54). After Patroclus' death they wept motionless on the battlefield 'like a gravestone', their manes in the dust (17.426-40), and Xanthus later spoke to Akhilleus to foretell his death (19.404-17). Their grief is now recalled as the reason Akhilleus stays out of the contest: they have lost 'so glorious a charioteer', who used to wash them and pour oil on their manes. Akhilleus also explains that they are a gift of Poseidon to Peleus; Leaf notes that this is one of the very few places where Homer connects Poseidon with horses, though later Greeks worshipped him as Poseidon Hippios. By withdrawing from his own games Akhilleus keeps the role of host and judge rather than competitor.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 23.277 and 23.283
N. J. Richardson, The Iliad: A Commentary, vol. 6: Books 21-24 (Cambridge, 1993), notes on 23.272-86

title: Eumelus, son of Admetus, and Apollo's mares
greek: ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Εὔμηλος (anax andrōn Eumēlos)
short: Eumelus drives the best mares in the army, bred by Apollo; Apollo helps him, Athena wrecks his chariot, and he comes in last.
body: Eumelus is the son of Admetus and Alcestis and leads the men of Pherae in Thessaly (2.711-15). The Catalogue calls his mares the best in the army, reared by Apollo himself in Pereia (2.763-7), which explains why Apollo knocks the whip from Diomedes' hand to keep them ahead (23.383-4); Leaf notes this link between Apollo and horse-breeding. Athena, who favours Diomedes, returns the whip and then breaks Eumelus' yoke, so that he is thrown out and his face skinned. The episode shows how divine partisanship continues even in sport, and both sides of it fit patterns from the battle books. It also leads to the first dispute of the games, when Akhilleus proposes giving the fallen Eumelus the second prize out of pity and Antilochus objects (23.536-54). Apart from the Catalogue, Eumelus appears only in this book.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 23.288 and 23.383
N. J. Richardson, The Iliad: A Commentary, vol. 6: Books 21-24 (Cambridge, 1993), notes on 23.288-9 and 23.382-400

title: Aethe and Echepolus: buying exemption from the war
greek: Αἴθην τὴν Ἀγαμεμνονέην (Aithēn tēn Agamemnoneēn)
short: Menelaus drives Agamemnon's mare Aethe, given by a rich man of Sicyon so that he would not have to go to Troy.
body: Aethe means 'Blaze' or 'Bright'. Echepolus, son of Anchises (not Aeneas' father), gave her to Agamemnon as a gift (dōron) so that he could stay at home in wealthy Sicyon and 'take his joy' instead of following him to 'windy Ilios'. The aside shows that service in the expedition was owed to Agamemnon and could be commuted by payment; Leaf compares Euchenor of Corinth, who chose to go to war rather than pay the penalty for staying behind (13.663-70). The detail is quietly ironic. Agamemnon's wealth comes partly from men who avoided the war, while the poem honours those who came and died. The mare is the best horse in Menelaus' team, and her 'goodly mettle' almost lets Menelaus catch Antilochus at the finish (23.524-7).

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 23.297

title: Nestor's lesson in mētis (cunning intelligence)
greek: μήτι τοι δρυτόμος μέγ' ἀμείνων ἠὲ βίηφι (mēti toi drytomos meg' ameinōn ēe biēphi)
short: Nestor tells Antilochus that skill and cunning (mētis), not strength (biē), make the woodcutter, the helmsman and the charioteer win.
body: Antilochus has the slowest horses, so his father advises mētis, the practical intelligence of the craftsman, sailor and trickster. The speech is built on a triple anaphora, mēti ... mēti ... mēti, and contrasts mētis with biē, force: the old opposition of Odysseus (polymētis) and Akhilleus (the 'best' in strength). Marcel Detienne and Jean-Pierre Vernant open their study of Greek cunning intelligence with this race, as the clearest literary model of mētis in action. Leaf, by contrast, thought the whole speech a later 'didactic' insertion, obscure and unrelated to the race, since the turning-post plays no part in what follows; Douglas Frame answers that the speech evokes Nestor's own past races. Antilochus does use cunning, but not at the turn: he takes a risk in a narrow gully, and the race ends with the question of whether his mētis was fair.

sources.cite: Marcel Detienne and Jean-Pierre Vernant, Cunning Intelligence in Greek Culture and Society, trans. Janet Lloyd (Hassocks: Harvester, 1978), Part I, 'Antilochus' race'
Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), Introduction to Book XXIII, p. 468
Douglas Frame, Hippota Nestor (Washington, DC: Center for Hellenic Studies, 2009), ch. 5
LSJ s.v. μῆτις

title: The turning-post: a sign (sēma) that may be a tomb
greek: ἤ τευ σῆμα βροτοῖο πάλαι κατατεθνηῶτος (ē teu sēma brotoio palai katatethnēōtos)
short: Nestor's landmark, a dry stump with two white stones, is either the tomb of a man long dead or an old turning-post: the word sēma means both 'sign' and 'grave'.
body: Nestor promises his son a sēma, a 'sign' he cannot miss, then describes a stump 'a fathom high' flanked by white stones, which may be 'the sēma of some mortal long ago dead' or a turning-post of men of old. Leaf found the passage hopelessly obscure, and notes that Aristotle (Poetics 25) records ancient critics who objected that wood would rot in the rain. Gregory Nagy reads the double meaning as deliberate: the race is run in honour of a dead hero, the great barrow of Patroclus (and Akhilleus) is being built nearby, and in Greek practice a hero's tomb could serve as a turning-post. Recognising the sign is an act of noēsis, interpretation. Douglas Frame relates the speech to Nestor's own earlier races. Whatever the answer, the passage makes the racecourse itself a place of memory for the dead.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 23.326, 23.331, 23.333
Gregory Nagy, 'Sēma and Noēsis: Some Illustrations', Arethusa 16 (1983); repr. in Greek Mythology and Poetics (Ithaca, 1990), ch. 8; summarised in The Ancient Greek Hero in 24 Hours, Hour 7
Douglas Frame, Hippota Nestor (CHS, 2009), ch. 5
Aristotle, Poetics 25, 1461a

anchor: Arion, the swift horse of Adrastus
title: Arion, the divine horse of Adrastus
greek: Ἀρίονα δῖον ... Ἀδρήστου ταχὺν ἵππον (Ariona dion ... Adrēstou tachyn hippon)
short: Nestor's example of an unbeatable horse: Arion, 'of divine stock', who carried Adrastus, leader of the Seven against Thebes, to safety.
body: Arion belongs to the Theban saga, which Homer knows but rarely tells. Adrastus, king of Argos, led the Seven against Thebes and alone survived, carried off by his marvellous horse. Pausanias (8.25.7-10) records the Arcadian story that Poseidon, in the form of a stallion, mated with Demeter, who had turned herself into a mare, and that Arion was their offspring; he quotes the epic Thebaid and the poet Antimachus on the horse's divine birth. Leaf notes that Arion was a favourite of the Theban cycle, endowed in later tradition with reason and speech (Propertius calls him 'vocalis Arion'), but outside Homer's usual world. Nestor adds the horses of Laomedon, the Trojan breed given by Zeus (5.265-72). The allusion places Antilochus' modest team beside the most famous horses of legend.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 23.346
Pausanias, Description of Greece 8.25.7-10
Propertius 2.34.37

anchor: narrow place in the hollow road
title: Antilochus' manoeuvre in the gully
greek: στεῖνος ὁδοῦ κοίλης (steinos hodou koilēs)
short: Where winter rain has cut the track, Antilochus drives alongside Menelaus, forcing him to pull back or risk a crash.
body: The road narrows where a winter torrent has broken it; Leaf explains that in such country a gully serves as road and stream bed by turns, with room for only one chariot. Menelaus keeps to the track 'to avoid the wheel-ruts' (or 'collision'), and Antilochus swerves alongside, 'as if he did not hear' Menelaus' warning. Menelaus gives way rather than risk wrecking both chariots, and loses second place. Homer measures the gap with a sporting image, the distance of a discus thrown from the shoulder (23.431). Whether Antilochus broke a rule is the question the later dispute turns on. Michael Gagarin argued that his tactic was within the rules of the race and that Menelaus' complaint rests on its danger and on his own status; others see clear foul play. The poem lets both men speak and lets the community, and the reader, judge.

title: The spectators' quarrel: Idomeneus, Aias and the histōr
greek: ἴστορα δ' Ἀτρεΐδην Ἀγαμέμνονα θείομεν ἄμφω (histora d' Atreïdēn Agamemnona theiomen amphō)
short: Two spectators argue over who is leading and propose a wager, with Agamemnon as histōr (umpire): a comic mirror of the quarrel in Book I.
body: Idomeneus, sitting high up, claims Diomedes is now in front; Aias son of Oïleus insults him as a braggart, and Idomeneus proposes a bet of a tripod or cauldron, with Agamemnon as histōr. The word, from the root of 'to know', means one who knows the facts and can judge; it also appears in the trial scene on the shield of Akhilleus (18.501), and it is the ancestor of historia, 'inquiry'. Akhilleus had already set Phoenix at the turning-post as a skopos, a watcher, 'to report the truth' (23.359-61). Leaf notes the scene can be cut without loss, yet admits it lets us see the race from the stands. It also replays Book I in miniature: an angry exchange of insults between chiefs, ended this time by Akhilleus himself, who tells both men to sit down and wait (23.490-8). The scholia note the irony that Aias accuses another of boasting.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), Introduction to Book XXIII, p. 468, and notes on 23.473-86

title: Akhilleus smiles at Antilochus
greek: μείδησεν δὲ ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς (meidēsen de podarkēs dios Achilleus)
short: The only time Akhilleus smiles in the Iliad: Antilochus refuses to give up his prize to Eumelus, and Akhilleus, pleased, finds Eumelus another.
body: Akhilleus proposes giving the second prize to Eumelus out of pity; Antilochus protests, in terms close to Akhilleus' own complaint in Book I, that his prize should not be taken from him, and offers to fight for it. Instead of anger, Akhilleus 'smiled, rejoicing in Antilochus, because he was his dear comrade'. It is his only smile in the poem. The moment reverses Book I: a dispute over a prize is settled by generosity from the hero's own store, here the bronze corselet of Asteropaeus (21.139-83). Antilochus is the friend who brought Akhilleus the news of Patroclus' death (18.1-21), and later tradition made him Akhilleus' closest companion after Patroclus, buried near them (Od. 24.78-9). The smile marks the first sign of Akhilleus returning to ordinary social life.

title: Menelaus' challenge: sceptre, themis and oath
greek: ἣ θέμις ἐστί (hē themis esti); ὄμνυθι (omnythi, 'swear')
short: Menelaus takes the speaker's staff, asks the chiefs to judge, then challenges Antilochus to swear by Poseidon that he used no trickery; Antilochus yields instead.
body: The scene is a small lawsuit. A herald puts the skēptron, the staff that gives a speaker the right to address the assembly, into Menelaus' hand and calls for silence. Menelaus first asks the leaders to judge 'without favour', then proposes to settle it himself by the customary procedure (themis): Antilochus must stand before his horses, hold the whip, touch the horses and swear by Poseidon, earth-holder and earth-shaker, that he did not hinder the chariot 'by guile' (dolos). Leaf notes Poseidon is the natural god for Antilochus, a descendant of Neleus son of Poseidon. Antilochus declines to swear, apologises on account of his youth and hands over the mare; Menelaus, touched, gives it back. David Mirhady and Michael Gagarin use the episode as early evidence for the oath-challenge in Greek dispute settlement. The quarrel that destroyed the army in Book I is here resolved by apology and generosity.

title: Simile: Menelaus' heart and the dew on the corn
greek: ὡς εἴ τε περὶ σταχύεσσιν ἐέρση (hōs ei te peri stachyessin eersē)
short: Menelaus' anger melts like dew warming the ears of ripening corn: a rare peaceful simile, followed by the narrator addressing Menelaus directly.
body: Most Iliad similes compare fighting to violent nature; this one compares relief to growth. Menelaus' heart is 'warmed' or 'cheered' (iainō) as dew on the ears of growing corn when the fields 'bristle'. Leaf discusses the grammar and reads it as 'his heart was gladdened as (the heart) of growing corn is gladdened with the dew'. The next line turns to Menelaus in the second person, 'so, Menelaus, was the heart in your breast cheered', an apostrophe used for Menelaus several times in the poem (for example 4.127, 7.104, 17.679) and for Patroclus in Book XVI; scholars read it as a mark of the narrator's sympathy. The softening of Menelaus prepares his graceful speech of forgiveness, in which he gives back the mare he has just won.

title: Akhilleus' gift to Nestor and the old man's honour
greek: Πατρόκλοιο τάφου μνῆμ' ἔμμεναι (Patrokloio taphou mnēm' emmenai)
short: Akhilleus gives the unclaimed fifth prize to Nestor as a keepsake of the funeral; Nestor answers with memories of his own victories at the games for Amarynceus.
body: The two-handled bowl is to be a keimēlion (treasure) and a mnēma (memorial) of Patroclus' funeral: the games are already turning grief into things that remember. Akhilleus gives it 'without a contest' (autōs) because age has made Nestor unable to compete. Nestor is delighted that he is remembered and receives the timē (honour) 'that it is fitting I should have among the Achaeans' (23.648-9). Timē here is given freely, the opposite of its forced removal in Book I. His reply turns into one of his characteristic reminiscences: at the funeral games for Amarynceus at Buprasium in Elis he won the boxing, wrestling, foot race and spear-throw, losing only the chariot race to the twin sons of Actor, who crowded him with their numbers. The scholia report that Aristarchus, citing Hesiod, took these twins, the Moliones, to be joined in one body. Leaf calls the couplet on their tactics beyond interpretation.

title: Epeius the boxer, later builder of the Wooden Horse
greek: υἱὸς Πανοπῆος Ἐπειός (huios Panopēos Epeios)
short: Epeius boasts he is poor in battle but best at boxing; in later legend he built the Wooden Horse that took Troy.
body: Epeius appears in the Iliad only in these games (also 23.839-40, where his throw is laughed at). He frankly admits he 'falls short in battle' but claims the boxing prize, a mule, and threatens to crush any challenger. He floors Euryalus with one blow and then, sportingly, sets him on his feet. Later tradition, known already to the Odyssey, made him the craftsman who built the Wooden Horse with Athena's help (Od. 8.492-3, 11.523). Leaf notes that the later fame comes from those passages. Plato's Myth of Er (Republic 10.620c) has Epeius' soul choose to be reborn as a woman skilled in crafts. The boxers fight with thongs of oxhide wound round the hands; Leaf explains anaschomenō as the technical term for 'squaring up'.

title: Euryalus and the funeral games of Oedipus
greek: Θήβας δ' ἦλθε δεδουπότος Οἰδιπόδαο ἐς τάφον (Thēbas d' ēlthe dedoupotos Oidipodao es taphon)
short: Euryalus' father Mecisteus once beat all the Thebans at the funeral games for Oedipus: an older version in which Oedipus died as king at Thebes.
body: Euryalus is the third leader of the Argive contingent under Diomedes (2.565-6). His father Mecisteus, brother of Adrastus, competed at the games for Oedipus 'when he had fallen' (dedoupotos, a word used of warriors falling in battle). This assumes a version of the legend in which Oedipus remained king at Thebes after the discovery of his crime and died there, the version also implied by the Odyssey, where Epicaste (Jocasta) hangs herself but Oedipus goes on ruling 'in sorrow' (Od. 11.271-80). The familiar story of his blinding, exile and death at Colonus near Athens is largely the work of Attic tragedy, especially Sophocles. Leaf points to Pausanias, who was told the bones had been brought to Attica from Thebes (1.28.7). The line is a precious glimpse of pre-tragic Theban myth.

title: Simile: the knocked-out boxer and the leaping fish
greek: ὡς δ' ὅθ' ὑπὸ φρικὸς Βορέω ἀναπάλλεται ἰχθύς (hōs d' hoth' hypo phrikos Boreō anapalletai ichthys)
short: Euryalus, struck on the jaw, leaps backwards like a fish that jumps on a weedy beach when the North Wind ruffles the water.
body: The simile catches a precise physical moment. The phrikē is the dark ripple a gust of wind raises on calm water; a fish leaps up in the shallows by the seaweed, and a dark wave closes over it. Leaf explains the apparent contradiction with the previous line, where Euryalus collapses on the spot: the blow lifts him clean off his feet, his body arches backward like a leaping fish, and he falls. The 'black wave' that hides the fish suggests the darkness of unconsciousness. The image fits the sporting context: a violent knock-out pictured through a small, natural, not deadly event. Afterwards Euryalus is led away 'spitting thick blood, his head lolling', one of the most realistic descriptions of a sports injury in ancient literature.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 23.692

title: The wrestling of Aias and Odysseus
greek: ὡς ὅτ' ἀμείβοντες, τούς τε κλυτὸς ἤραρε τέκτων (hōs hot' ameibontes, tous te klytos ērare tektōn)
short: Great Aias and cunning Odysseus lock together like the rafters of a roof; neither can win, and Akhilleus declares a draw.
body: The prizes are valued in oxen, the standard measure of worth: a tripod worth twelve oxen for the winner, a skilled woman worth four for the loser. Leaf notes how low that valuation is beside the twenty oxen Laertes paid for Eurycleia (Od. 1.431). The wrestlers grip each other 'like rafters' (ameibontes) that a builder joins at the roof-peak to resist the wind: a picture of two equal forces locked in balance. The match pits Aias' strength against Odysseus' 'cunning' (kerdea, 23.709): Odysseus kicks the back of Aias' knee and brings him down. Later epic tells how the same two men competed for the arms of the dead Akhilleus, a contest that Odysseus won and that drove Aias to suicide (Od. 11.543-64). Here Akhilleus stops the bout and gives them equal prizes, the kind of fair settlement that contest will lack.

title: The Sidonian silver mixing-bowl: the biography of an object
greek: ἀργύρεον κρητῆρα τετυγμένον (argyreon krētēra tetygmenon)
short: The foot-race prize, a silver bowl made by Sidonians, carried by Phoenician traders, given to Thoas of Lemnos, and paid to Patroclus as ransom for Lycaon.
body: Homer often gives a precious object a history, which adds to its worth. This bowl was made by Sidonian craftsmen, 'skilled in many arts', carried over the sea by Phoenician merchants, given to Thoas, king of Lemnos, and paid by his grandson Euneos (son of Jason and Hypsipyle) to Patroclus as the price of Lycaon, the son of Priam whom Akhilleus had sold into slavery on Lemnos (21.34-44). Leaf notes that Homer consistently distinguishes the Sidonians as craftsmen from the Phoenicians as traders; the Odyssey has a similar Sidonian bowl given to Menelaus (Od. 4.615-19). The bowl carries the story of a ransom that saved a Trojan's life for a time; Lycaon later met Akhilleus again and was killed (21.34-135). Prized objects thus link the games to the human cost of the war.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 23.741-6

title: Simile: Odysseus close as the weaving-rod to a woman's breast
greek: στήθεός ἐστι κανών (stētheos esti kanōn)
short: Odysseus runs as close behind Aias as the rod is to a weaving woman's breast as she draws the spool across the warp.
body: The simile comes from the women's world of the house, rare in the Iliad. Leaf follows Hugo Blümner's explanation of the upright Greek loom: the warp threads hung down from a beam, attached alternately to rods (kanones); pulling a rod towards her chest opened a gap through which the weaver passed the spool (pēnion) with the weft. The point of comparison is the tiny, constant distance between the rod and her breast. The domestic image prepares the comic sequel, in which Athena is called Odysseus' 'mother' (23.783). Odysseus' feet fall in Aias' footprints 'before the dust had settled' and his breath beats on Aias' head, so the simile measures closeness both in space and in effort.

title: Athena 'like a mother' to Odysseus; the slip of Aias
greek: μήτηρ ὣς Ὀδυσῆϊ παρίσταται ἠδ' ἐπαρήγει (mētēr hōs Odysēï paristatai ēd' eparēgei)
short: Odysseus prays; Athena makes Aias slip in the dung of the sacrificed bulls, and the loser complains that she stands by Odysseus 'like a mother'.
body: Odysseus prays silently to Athena; she lightens his limbs and trips Aias, son of Oïleus, who falls face-first in dung from the oxen slaughtered for Patroclus. The army laughs at him. His complaint names the special bond of Athena and Odysseus that the Odyssey will develop at length; Nestor there says he never saw the gods show love so openly (Od. 3.218-22). Virgil imitated the fall in his foot race, where Nisus slips in the blood of sacrifices (Aen. 5.327-33). Antilochus, taking the last prize, makes a graceful speech: the gods honour older men; Odysseus is of an earlier generation, in 'green old age' (ōmogerōn), and hard to beat by anyone but Akhilleus. Leaf compares Virgil's 'cruda deo viridisque senectus' (Aen. 6.304). His compliment earns him an extra half-talent.

title: The iron weight of Eëtion
greek: σόλον αὐτοχόωνον (solon autochoōnon)
short: The weight thrown in the contest is itself the prize: a lump of iron, once Eëtion's, enough to supply a farm for five years.
body: The solos is a mass of iron 'cast by itself'; Leaf takes it to mean pig-iron just as it came from the smelting furnace, noting that some have thought of meteoric iron. It belonged to Eëtion, king of Thebe under Plakos and father of Andromache, whom Akhilleus killed when he sacked the city (6.414-24). Akhilleus stresses its practical value: the winner's shepherd and ploughman will not need to go to town for iron for five years. In Homer bronze is the metal of weapons and iron is still scarce and precious, often listed among treasures (6.48); the passage reflects a world that knew iron tools. The comrades of Polypoetes, who throws it furthest, carry it off. Leaf thought the whole contest obscure, but the prize's history again links the games to Akhilleus' earlier conquests.

sources.cite: Walter Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2: Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), notes on 23.826 and 23.832

title: The archery contest: a vow to Apollo
greek: τρήρωνα πέλειαν (trērōna peleian)
short: Teucer forgets to vow a hecatomb to Apollo and only cuts the cord; Meriones vows and kills the dove in flight.
body: A dove is tied by the foot to a ship's mast set up in the sand; hitting the bird wins ten double axes, cutting the cord wins ten single ones. Teucer, the best archer among the Achaeans, shoots first but 'did not vow to the lord' a hecatomb of firstling lambs, and Apollo grudges him the hit. Meriones snatches the bow, makes the vow and brings the dove down. The lesson is religious: the archer-god Apollo must be acknowledged; Leaf notes that the hecatomb of lambs seems to be his fixed price for a successful shot. Leaf also found the contest absurd, since the second prize rewards a pure accident. Virgil copied it closely in Aeneid V (485-518), where the cord is cut and the bird then shot, and Walter Scott used the motif in Anne of Geierstein.

title: The javelin: Akhilleus honours Agamemnon
greek: ἴδμεν γὰρ ὅσον προβέβηκας ἁπάντων (idmen gar hoson probebēkas hapantōn)
short: The last contest is not held: Akhilleus awards the first prize to Agamemnon as the acknowledged best, and Agamemnon accepts.
body: Agamemnon and Meriones stand up for the javelin, but Akhilleus declares that everyone knows how far Agamemnon surpasses all 'in might and in throwing'. He gives him the cauldron and Meriones the spear, and Agamemnon agrees. The closing gesture answers Book I, where Agamemnon took Akhilleus' prize and Akhilleus insisted that he himself was 'the best of the Achaeans' (1.244). Now Akhilleus, master of the games, publicly gives Agamemnon a prize and the title of best without a contest. Readers have argued whether this is reconciliation, courtesy or quiet irony, since Agamemnon has never been praised as a spearman. Leaf notes difficulties about which prize is which. Agamemnon hands his prize to Talthybius, the herald who led Briseis away in Book I (1.320-48). The games end in agreement, preparing for Book XXIV.
